sections.title: Part Ⅰ TASK A. Readback and Hearback

body.label: Ground
body.text: HL123, give way to the Boeing 787 on Charlie.

body.label: Tower
body.text: HL123, traffic is an ATR on final, cleared for immediate takeoff runway 08, report passing 3,000 feet.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, descend to 4,000 feet, cleared for the RNAV runway 26 approach, contact Halston Tower on 120.35.

body.label: Delivery
body.text: HL123, cleared to Halston Airport via the CANTO TWO departure, maintain 6,000 feet, squawk 2046.

sections.title: Part Ⅰ TASK B. Checking, Clarifying, Confirming, Informing

body.text: You are holding over OBLIN while the controller sorts out the arrival sequence. You have one hour 20 minutes of fuel on board, and your alternate needs 40 minutes. Now ATC contacts you. Provide both pieces of information.

body.label: Center
body.text: HL123, say your endurance, and how many more turns in the hold you can take.

On final into Everett last night you were hit by a green laser from the left of the approach path, at about 600 feet. You were too busy to report it then. You have now landed and the ground controller calls you. Acknowledge the taxi instruction, and report what happened on the approach.

body.label: Ground
body.text: HL123, Everett Ground, taxi to stand 24 via Bravo.

Approach instructed you to maintain heading 070. A build-up appeared ahead, so you turned 20 degrees right to avoid it and you are now steady on heading 090. Now ATC contacts you. Respond accordingly.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, confirm maintaining heading 070?
heading 090 / weather avoidance

The controller has cleared you direct ZAVER. Your weather radar shows a line of storms sitting right on that track, with tops above your level, and you can only take that routing after you are past the line. Listen to the controller, respond with a reason, and tell him what you can accept instead.

body.label: Center
body.text: HL123, cleared direct ZAVER.
Delivery gave you squawk 2046 before departure. You set 2064 in the transponder by mistake and it has been running that way since take-off. Now ATC contacts you. Respond accordingly.

body.label: Center
body.text: HL123, verify your squawk.

Your arrival chart shows a crossing restriction of 11,000 feet at MERIS, but the controller has cleared you to descend to flight level 120, which leaves you above that restriction. You are 30 miles from MERIS. Contact Halston Approach. Point out the difference, and request the descent you need.
MERIS 11,000 feet

sections.title: Part Ⅱ TASK A. Role-play & Follow-up

pre.text: Flight Paths In this scenario, you'll be the pilot flying HL123, which goes through 3 flight stages: Climb, Cruise, Diversion.
Initial Situation You are the pilot of HL123, climbing through 12,000 feet for flight level 330, departed from Everett and bound for Halston.

body.text: Contact Northfield Control and report your position.
Listen to the controller and give a full readback.

body.label: Center
body.text: HL123, Northfield Control, radar contact, climb and maintain flight level 330, after CANTO cleared direct MERIS.

pre.text: Situation Update You are level at flight level 330. The cabin crew call to tell you a passenger has collapsed and is not responding well. A doctor on board is attending.

body.text: Inform the controller of the situation, state that you are considering a diversion, and request the weather at the nearest suitable airport.
Listen to the controller, give a readback of the weather, and state your intentions with a reason.

body.label: Center
body.text: HL123, roger, the nearest suitable is Redwood, 60 miles south-east, wind 240 at 8, visibility 10 kilometres, runway 26 is 2,600 metres. Halston is 140 miles ahead. Say your intentions.

pre.text: Situation Update You have decided to divert to Redwood and the company agrees. The doctor says the passenger should be on the ground within the hour.

body.text: Contact Northfield Control, request descent and direct Redwood, and request priority handling with an ambulance on arrival.
Listen to the controller and give a full readback.

body.label: Center
body.text: HL123, roger, descend to flight level 180, direct Redwood, contact Redwood Approach on 126.9. Your ambulance request is passed on.

pre.text: Situation Update You are now descending through flight level 190 for 11,000 feet. There are 178 passengers and 8 crew on board.

body.text: Contact Redwood Approach and report your passing altitude.
Listen to the controller and give a full readback.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, Redwood Approach, descend to 3,000 feet, reduce speed to 180 knots, cleared for the ILS runway 26 approach, report established.
Listen to the controller and provide both pieces of information.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, two things — how many people are on board, and do you need the ambulance at the gate or on the runway?
Listen to the tower and give a full readback. Then inquire where the ambulance will meet you.

body.label: Tower
body.text: HL123, Redwood Tower, wind 250 at 10, runway 26, cleared to land, the ambulance is standing by.

Follow-up question: You have just finished Task A, as the pilot of Hotel Lima one two three. In this situation, you chose to divert to Redwood instead of continuing to Halston. What did you weigh up before you made that choice? In your role as a pilot, how do you decide whether a sick passenger is a reason to divert? Give an example of a case where you would keep going instead.

sections.title: Part Ⅱ TASK B. Extended Role-play : Single Incident/Emergency Related

pre.text: Initial Situation You are the pilot of HL123, descending through flight level 160 for 9,000 feet, inbound to Halston Airport. You have information Bravo.

body.text: Contact Halston Approach and report your position.
Listen to the controller and give a full readback.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, Halston Approach, good evening, descend and maintain 9,000 feet, reduce speed to 220 knots, expect the MERIS ONE arrival, ILS runway 08, Halston altimeter 29.88.

pre.text: Situation Update Selecting flap for the approach, the flaps stop at 15 and will not move any further. The checklist tells you to plan a flaps 15 landing — your approach speed will be 165 knots and you will need 2,400 metres of landing distance.

body.text: Inform the controller of your situation, state that you are maintaining 9,000 feet, and request time to work the checklist.
Listen to the controller, give a full readback and say your intentions.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, roger, fly heading 120 and maintain 9,000 feet, that will keep you clear of the arrivals. Say your intentions when you are ready.
Listen to the controller and provide both pieces of information.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, two questions — what is your approach speed with flaps 15, and how much landing distance do you need?
Listen to the controller. Tell him what you need to know before you decide, then state your intentions with a reason.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, runway 08 is 2,300 metres, so that is tight for you. Runway 26 is 3,000 metres but you would have a 15 knot tailwind. Which do you want?

pre.text: Situation Update The tower reports the wind is now 080 at 6, so the tailwind on runway 26 has gone. You have finished the checklist.

body.text: Contact approach, give them an update, state your decision, and say what you will need on landing.
Listen to the controller and give a full readback.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, roger, turn right heading 350, descend to 2,500 feet until established, cleared for the ILS runway 26 approach, contact Halston Tower on 120.35.
Listen to the controller and provide both pieces of information.

body.label: Approach
body.text: HL123, the tower is asking two things — will you be able to vacate at the end, and do you want the fire service to follow you in?

body.text: What happened to your aircraft (HL123)? Explain the nature of the incident.
How do you think the incident was handled by the air traffic controller? Do you feel the situation could have been handled differently? Make a comment from a pilot's point of view.
